structure.overview: The case involves Applicants seeking judicial review of the Temporary Public Policy (CUAET) on grounds of alleged discrimination under section 15 of the Charter, against the Respondent Attorney General. The Respondent moved to be relieved from filing a full Certified Tribunal Record (CTR), arguing only legal questions are at issue, not specific decisions. The Court partially granted the motion, requiring production of relevant CUAET documents but excluding unrelated LCA and individual decision documents.

party_points.text: no specific decision challenged, only legal question
CUAET discriminates based on nationality contrary to section 15 Charter
CUAET provides better benefits than LCA policy for Afghan nationals
seek documents on CUAET, LCA, and refusals for family members
documents relevant to assess discrimination and Charter defences
challenge CUAET legality under section 15 but not Minister's decisions
documents needed to assess Charter challenge including sections 15(2) and 1

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Respondent AG moves to be relieved from filing a Certified Tribunal Record as required by the Court's April 23, 2024 Production Order under Rule 14(2).
idea_list: AG's motion to be relieved from filing CTR
AG objects to electronic sending requirement

citations.cite: Rule 14(2) of the Federal Courts Citizenship, Immigration and Refugee Protection Rules, SOR/93-22
citations.why: AG relies on this rule to seek relief from filing CTR

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicants seek judicial review of the Temporary Public Policy (CUAET), alleging it is unconstitutional due to discrimination.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The AG argues the Applicants do not challenge a specific decision requiring a CTR, only a legal question answerable by existing evidence and arguments.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court partially grants the motion, relieving the AG from producing documents unrelated to the challenged CUAET but requiring CTR for relevant CUAET documents.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicants are Canadian citizens with Afghan family abroad, alleging CUAET discriminates based on nationality contrary to section 15 of the Charter.

citations.cite: section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicants argue CUAET provides better benefits than the LCA policy for Afghan nationals; they do not challenge individual immigration decisions.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicants oppose the motion, seeking documents the Minister considered in making CUAET, LCA, and refusing LCA applications for specific family members.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicants say these documents are relevant to determine if CUAET is discriminatory and to assess Charter violation defences under sections 15(2) and 1.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Rule 14(2) must be read with Rule 17(b), which requires a CTR to include all relevant documents in the tribunal's possession.

citations.cite: Abu v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 1031 at para 40
citations.why: Supports interpretation of Rule 17(b) requiring relevant documents in CTR

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The relevance test under Rule 17 matches that under Rule 317 of Federal Courts Rules: documents relevant if they may affect the Court's decision.

citations.cite: Douze v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 1086 at para 19
Nguesso v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 102 at para 94

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court routinely issues production orders before leave to allow time for settlement, consistent with IRPA section 74 and practice guidelines.

citations.why: Supports early production orders for settlement

citations.cite: Consolidated Practice Guidelines for Citizenship, Immigration, and Refugee Protection Proceedings dated June 24, 2022 (last amended October 31, 2023) at para 40
citations.why: Practice guidelines supporting early production orders

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Applicants challenge CUAET's legality under section 15 Charter but do not challenge any Minister's decision or interpretation under IRPA subsection 25.2(1).

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicants contend documents sought are needed to assess the Charter challenge, including whether distinctions are justified under sections 15(2) or 1.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court agrees documents about CUAET's development are relevant; unlike CARL, here relevancy of documents is established for the Charter challenge.
idea_list: Court agrees documents on CUAET relevant
Distinguishes CARL case where relevancy not established

citations.cite: Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 128 [CARL]
citations.why: Distinguished CARL where no relevancy of documents shown

citations.cite: Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1204

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Section 15(2) and section 1 require courts to determine the law's objective; proof of discriminatory intent is not required but CTR may assist assessment.

citations.cite: Law v Canada, [1999] 1 SCR 497 at para 80
citations.why: Supports requirement to determine law's objective

citations.cite: Fraser v Canada (Attorney General), 2020 SCC 28 at paras 79-80
citations.why: Supports requirement to determine law's objective

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Supreme Court in Sharma recognized extrinsic evidence can help identify legislative purpose despite caution against reliance on it.

citations.why: Supports use of extrinsic evidence to assess legislative purpose

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: This Court follows similar approach ordering disclosure of documents considered in policy decisions, even if this is a constitutional challenge, not traditional judicial review.

citations.cite: Janssen Inc v Canada (Health), 2023 FC 870 at para 61
citations.why: Supports ordering disclosure of documents considered in policy decisions

citations.cite: Portnov v Canada (Attorney General), 2021 FCA 171 [Portnov] at paras 33‑34
citations.why: Supports ordering disclosure of documents considered in policy decisions

citations.cite: Canada Mink Breeders Association v British Columbia, 2022 BCSC 1731 at para 35
citations.why: Supports ordering disclosure of documents considered in policy decisions

citations.cite: Airth v Canada (National Revenue), 2007 FC 415 at para 7
citations.why: Supports ordering disclosure of documents considered in policy decisions

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Determining relevant documents is fact-specific; many documents relevant to judicial review of CUAET are also relevant to assessing its Charter legality.

citations.why: Documents shedding light on reasoning and submissions are relevant

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Respondent's Record includes an affidavit by Ms. Cato describing CUAET background and attaching publicly available documents.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The annexed documents are publicly available and do not include the information Applicants seek, which they should receive subject to exemptions.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court grants the motion in part, limiting CTR production to relevant CUAET information and excluding LCA-related documents and individual decisions.
